title: Don't Trash That Pumpkin: Give It a Second Life
summary:
Every fall, tens of millions of pumpkins show up on doorsteps and porches across the United States. Some become spooky jack-o'-lanterns. Others simply sit outside as decorations. Then Halloween ends, and for most people, the pumpkin's job is done.

But that goodbye comes with a big hidden cost. Experts estimate that over one billion pounds of pumpkins end up in landfills each year in the United States. That is more than 80 percent of the 1.3 billion pounds purchased annually. The problem is not only in the United States. In the United Kingdom, about 55 percent of the 39 million pumpkins bought for the holiday go uneaten, adding up to about $37 million worth of food.

When pumpkins rot in landfills, they release methane, a greenhouse gas that traps much more heat than carbon dioxide over a shorter period. So a decoration that looked harmless on a porch can add to climate change once it is thrown away.

Fortunately, there is an easy fix, and it starts before you toss anything. If a pumpkin was used as decor, scoop out the edible insides. Roasted pumpkin seeds make a nutritious and tasty snack. The flesh can become a hearty soup, a creamy puree, or a delicious pie. You can also donate pumpkins to local farms or zoos, where they can be used as animal feed.

If a pumpkin is too far gone to eat or donate, bury it in your yard. It will naturally decompose and add nutrients to the soil. Giving an old pumpkin a second life is a small choice, but multiplied across millions of homes, it can help reduce waste and protect our environment.
why_it_matters: Pumpkin waste is not just a Halloween leftover problem: rotting pumpkins in landfills add methane to the atmosphere, so reusing, donating, or burying them is a small everyday choice that, multiplied across millions of homes, can reduce waste and help protect the environment.

background_read: A pumpkin is a large orange fruit that grows in the fall and is often carved into a jack-o'-lantern or used as a decoration for Halloween.
After the holiday, many pumpkins are thrown away, and when food rots in a landfill without much air, it can release methane, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.
Instead of throwing a pumpkin away, its seeds and flesh can be eaten, it can be given to animals as feed, or it can be buried or composted so it breaks down and returns nutrients to the soil.
